extraction.method: Extract every physical PDF page to a UTF-8 text file with an explicit PDF-page marker. SHA256 covers the original acquired PDF bytes and the complete extracted UTF-8 text bytes.
extraction.integrity_scope: Hashes verify the cached bytes only. They do not by themselves verify mathematical correctness or prove that every extracted glyph was legible.

documents.title: Statistics for Applications: complete lecture notes
documents.author: Dmitry Panchenko
documents.institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, MIT OpenCourseWare
documents.edition: Course lecture notes; no book edition stated
documents.license: The MIT OCW course record identifies the course as Creative Commons BY-NC-SA. The PDF copy was fetched from an OCW mirror because the old resource endpoint was not directly accessible.
documents.reading_status: Complete relevant lecture units read; the full 139-page source was acquired and extracted, but unrelated chapters were not counted as read.
anchors: Lecture 1, pp. 1-2: model questions, estimation and testing framing.
Lecture 3, pp. 8-12: method-of-moments estimator and its conditions.
Lectures 6-7, pp. 25-31: Cauchy-Schwarz proof of Rao-Cramer; equality condition and efficiency.
Lecture 12, pp. 47-48: sufficient statistics and the Rao-Blackwell MSE proof.
Lecture 17, pp. 63-66: exact normal-theory confidence intervals from chi-square and Student pivots.
Lectures 18-22, pp. 67-88: simple/composite hypotheses, randomized most-powerful tests, MLR and one-sided UMP proof.
documents.assessment: Useful complete proof treatment for Rao-Blackwell, scalar Rao-Cramer, randomized most-powerful testing, one-sided MLR/UMP, and exact normal pivots. The Rao-Cramer proof differentiates the normalizing integral without stating a sufficiently explicit fixed-support/dominated-differentiation hypothesis; use the independent MIT 18.655 and Oxford regularity statements. The test definitions around Lectures 18-20 use inconsistent error/decision notation, so the dossier does not rely on this source for definitions or Neyman-Pearson proof. Its UMP proof is independently checked against Oxford and USC.

documents.title: Unbiased Estimation and Risk Inequalities
documents.author: Peter Kempthorne
documents.institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, MIT OpenCourseWare
documents.edition: Course lecture note; no edition stated
documents.license: MIT OpenCourseWare Creative Commons license, linked by the resource page.
anchors: PDF pp. 6-8: regular problem, fixed support, score identities and Fisher information.
PDF pp. 10-12: scalar information inequality and iid information additivity.
PDF pp. 13-15: equality characterization and regular one-parameter exponential-family conclusion.
PDF pp. 16-19: vector score and matrix information bounds.
documents.assessment: Primary independent treatment for CRLB regularity and proof: fixed support, finite score, and explicit differentiation-under-the-integral condition for integrable statistics. The scalar proof is covariance/score identity followed by Cauchy-Schwarz. Vector bounds require nonsingular information. No finite-sample bound is claimed for biased estimators without using the derivative of their mean.

anchors: PDF pp. 1-3: estimator, unbiasedness, estimability, MSE, finite-sample normal variance-divisor comparison.
PDF pp. 4-5: consistency and asymptotic normality; read but not used for this assignment.
documents.assessment: Good finite-sample comparison and counterexample source. The MSE calculation shows that the biased normal variance estimator using divisor n has smaller MSE than the unbiased estimator using n-1. The lecture's bootstrap and asymptotic discussion is outside this dossier's scope.

documents.title: Efficient Estimators, Rao-Cramer Bound
documents.author: Anna Mikusheva
documents.institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, MIT OpenCourseWare
documents.course_and_date: 14.381 Statistical Method in Economics, Fall 2018, Lecture 6
documents.edition: Course lecture note; no edition stated
documents.license: MIT OpenCourseWare Creative Commons license, linked by the course page.
documents.reading_status: Entire 7-page lecture unit read; PDF pp. 5-6 also visually inspected.
anchors: PDF pp. 3-5: support condition, derivative domination, score and information identities.
PDF pp. 5-6: Rao-Cramer theorem and Cauchy-Schwarz proof.
PDF p. 6: Uniform(0,theta) support-dependent counterexample.
documents.assessment: Useful independent scalar proof and counterexample. The printed Uniform example has an arithmetic typo: it writes 1/I_n(theta)=theta^2/n^2, whereas I_n=n/theta^2 gives theta^2/n. Its conclusion that the unbiased endpoint estimator beats the naive bound is still true. The proof's hypotheses require differentiation of the estimator mean under the integral; the theorem's rendered condition states this correctly.

documents.institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, MIT OpenCourseWare
documents.course_and_date: 14.381 Statistical Method in Economics, Fall 2018, Lecture 9
documents.edition: Course lecture note; no edition stated
documents.license: MIT OpenCourseWare Creative Commons license, linked by the course page.
documents.reading_status: Entire 7-page lecture unit read; PDF p. 5 visually inspected.
anchors: PDF pp. 3-4: UMP definition and Neyman-Pearson proof for simple hypotheses.
PDF pp. 4-5: MLR and Karlin-Rubin one-sided theorem.
PDF p. 5: theorem statement and proof orientation.
documents.assessment: Theorem 3 has a sign defect: for an increasing likelihood ratio and H0: theta >= theta0 versus H1: theta < theta0, the theorem statement gives an upper-tail rejection rule T>C, while its own proof correctly accepts for T>C and rejects for T<C. The correct lower-tail orientation is established independently by Oxford and USC. The two-sided normal example correctly illustrates that UMP tests need not exist.

anchors: Chapter 3, PDF pp. 22-24: common-support and derivative-interchange regularity, score, Fisher information, and score/Hessian identity.

The LS proof explicitly combines sufficiency, completeness, Rao-Blackwell and uniqueness. The UMP theorem assumes a continuous statistic to avoid boundary randomization; use a randomized threshold in the scaffold when a discrete statistic has an atom.
